newsitem.title: UK: Falklands "war without hate" - Argentine army chief.
newsitem.headline: Falklands "war without hate" - Argentine army chief.

text.p: Argentina's military chief, paying an emotional tribute to the dead on both sides in the Falklands confict, said on Wednesday it was a "war without hate".

General Martin Balza also praised the "bravery and professionalism" of British soldiers when paying the first visit to London by an Argentine armed forces chief since the two countries went to war in 1982 over the disputed South Atlantic islands.
Around 1,000 servicemen died in the 10-week war after Britain sent a task force to dislodge Argentine troops.
"It was a war without hate. The dignity of the conquered was respected," said Balza, an artillery officer who became a British prisoner of war for two weeks after the conflict.
Balza, who has been touring British garrisons and observing training exercises on his highly symbolic visit, said he was constantly asked after the war how the British treated him.
"Always the same. We were respected," he said, even if his prisoner of war diet seemed to consist largely of corn flakes.
Balza, the highest ranking officer to travel to London since the war, was the only top commander to survive a shake-up of Argentina's military high command last month.
"The best thing we must do for the soldiers who died in the South Atlantic conflict is to pray to give them eternal rest," he told a meeting of the Royal United Services Institute.

Balza's historic visit is viewed by Argentine officials as a bridge-mending exercise after the 1990 resumption of diplomatic links between the former foes. British and Argentine forces have served alongside each other as U.N. peacekeepers in Cyprus.
"I hope my visit here will improve the bond of friendship, understanding and confidence between our armies," Balza said.
He said of his reception during a three-day official visit to Britain at the invitation of British chief of staff Sir Charles Guthrie, "We really did feel as if we were at home."
The Argentine Army has been slashed to half its 1982 size, but he said the new-look force was more streamlined and effective. "One can be just as efficient by being small."
